canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Load line — conditions of assignment
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
To ensure compliance with load line assignment under ICLL 1966 and the UK Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Regulations 1998, inspection focuses on the vessel's watertight/weathertight integrity, structural strength and crew protection — together the "conditions of assignment" that must be maintained for the assigned freeboard to remain valid:

1. **Load line markings** — deck line, load line marks and draught marks clearly visible, correctly painted and positioned for the assigned freeboard.
2. **Hatchways and closures** — hatch covers on exposed decks weathertight, closing appliances/tarpaulins/securing devices sound; coaming heights correct for Position 1 vs Position 2.
3. **Machinery space openings** — engine room skylights, fiddley openings and casings with efficient weathertight closures.
4. **Manholes and flush scuttles** — watertight, capable of being secured.
5. **Ventilators and air pipes** — weathertight closing devices fitted and operable, coamings to required height.
6. **Side scuttles and deadlights** — watertight below the freeboard deck, packing free of cracks.
7. **Cargo ports and watertight doors** — all shell openings below the freeboard deck securely watertight.
8. **Scuppers, inlets and discharges** — non-return valves on overboard discharges functional.
9. **Freeing ports** — correct area for the length of bulwark served, non-return flaps free to operate.
10. **Bulwarks, guardrails and crew protection** — guard rails, lifelines, gangways and walkways sound, giving safe access between accommodation and machinery spaces.
11. **Structure and stability** — hull/frame/bulkhead integrity verified, stability documentation current.

Finally, confirm the assigned marks agree with the freeboard on a valid Load Line Certificate: check the certificate, the stability book, and confirm no structural alteration has changed the assigned freeboard.
examiner_focus: The marks sit in naming the specific ICLL/Load Line "conditions of assignment" checklist -- closing appliances, freeing ports, guard rails, deck line marks -- not a generic seaworthiness survey.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12/Q.13 · Panting & pounding
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Panting and pounding are distinct local, dynamic stresses acting forward of the collision bulkhead, caused by the ship's interaction with waves.

**Panting** — cyclic in-and-out flexing of the shell plating as the bow (and, less severely, the stern) alternately immerses and emerges while pitching. Affects the fore end from stem to collision bulkhead (~forward 15% L) and, to a lesser degree, the aft peak. Effects: fatigue cracking of plating/welds, separation of plating from stiffeners, structural deformation.

**Pounding (slamming)** — the bow lifts clear of the water in heavy head seas, especially light/ballast condition, then strikes the surface as a sudden impact load (not a pressure cycle). Affects the flat of bottom forward (~25–30% L) and the forward shoulder. Effects: dents, buckling, rupture of bottom plating, deformed floors/girders, and **whipping** — transient high-frequency vibration of the whole hull girder from the slam, raising stress throughout the length.

*Structure resisting panting:* panting stringers (triangular, ~2 m vertical spacing, to the collision bulkhead); panting beams at alternate frames tying port/starboard stringers; breast hooks at the stem; wash plates/wash bulkhead in the peak tank.

*Structure resisting pounding:* thickened bottom shell over the forward ~25–30% L; solid plate floors at every frame in that zone; intercostal side girders (≤~2.2 m apart); reduced frame spacing (~700 mm forward vs ~900 mm typical).

*Sketch variant (Oct 2024):* draw the forepeak elevation at centreline labelling panting stringers, panting beams, breast hooks, wash plates, deep floors and the solid round stem bar — marks are for correct labelling, not just outline accuracy.
examiner_focus: Panting is a cyclic pressure effect from pitching; pounding is a sudden slam impact, not a pressure cycle -- conflating the two mechanisms, or their affected zones (fore-end shell vs flat-of-bottom), is the main error.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Bilge keels — damage prevention, testing, length
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i)** Bilge keels are attached via a **ground bar** (an intercostal flat-bar doubler) continuously double-fillet welded to the shell plating over an internal longitudinal or frame — never directly to unsupported shell. The bilge keel is then welded to this ground bar, and that keel-to-ground-bar weld is the deliberately weaker joint: on impact the keel shears off there, leaving the shell plating intact. Design features protecting the shell:
- **Doubler/ground bar** — sacrificial buffer between keel and shell.
- **Weakened connection ("soft nose")** — the keel-to-doubler weld is the designed breaking point.
- **Internal stiffening alignment** — the ground bar lands on supported structure (frames/longitudinals), not flexible unsupported plating.
- **Soft, rounded/snipped ends** — tapered and aligned with internal structure, avoiding a hard spot and crack initiation.
- **Limited length** — restricted to ~30–60% of the ship's length amidships, avoiding the high stresses of the ends, and kept inside the moulded line of the bilge so it doesn't increase the ship's extreme breadth or draught.

**(a)(ii)** Testing: a solid bilge keel cannot be leak- or pressure-tested. Integrity is judged by visual inspection at dry dock plus crack testing (MPI or dye-penetrant) of the welds, hammer/percussion testing for detached sections, and checking weld toes for fatigue cracking.

**(b)** Reasons bilge keels don't run the full length:
1. Full-length keels would cause excessive frictional drag, raising fuel consumption and reducing speed.
2. The bow/stern are more exposed to damage (slamming, manoeuvring, docking) — full-length keels risk being torn off there.
3. Maximum roll damping occurs midships, where relative velocity between hull and water is greatest.
4. The keel must stay inside the moulded line of the bilge, avoiding any increase to extreme breadth/draught (grounding/quay-contact protection).
examiner_focus: A solid bilge keel cannot be leak- or pressure-tested -- examiners specifically check that candidates don't claim a hydrostatic test; the real answer is visual inspection plus NDT (MPI/dye-penetrant) at the welds.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Ship-construction terms (purpose & location)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a) Duct keel** — a longitudinal watertight tunnel in the double bottom of bulk carriers/container ships, running along the centreline from the collision bulkhead to the forward engine room bulkhead. Strengthens the bottom against longitudinal stress and houses ballast/fuel/bilge pipework. Clear width commonly limited to ~2 m so the double bottom either side stays effective; not carried under the machinery space (a solid centre girder is fitted there instead). An enclosed space — entry requires the full enclosed-space-entry procedure.

**b) Bilge keel** — a narrow fin/plate along the turn of the bilge, both sides, amidships. Increases hydrodynamic resistance (via eddy/vortex shedding) as the vessel rolls, damping roll amplitude.

**c) Collision bulkhead** — the foremost, heavily reinforced transverse watertight bulkhead, bottom to freeboard deck, restricting flooding from the forepeak in a head-on collision. Per SOLAS II-1/ICLL: sited not less than 0.05L (or 10 m, whichever is less) and not more than 0.08L (or 0.05L + 3 m) from the forward perpendicular at the load line — the loose "5–8% of L or 10 m max" phrasing conflates these two separate limits. No openings/doors below the freeboard deck; only one pipe penetration, with a screw-down valve operable from above, is allowed.

**d) Camber** — slight parabolic transverse curvature of exposed weather decks (classically B/50 at midships; modern ships often use straight-line camber), higher at centreline. Drains water off deck, adds structural strength against bending, and offsets the visual "hog" illusion.

**e) Flare** — outward curvature of the hull side shell rising from waterline to main deck, greatest at the bow. Deflects water from the deck, increases reserve buoyancy/deck area/stability — but excessive flare aggravates bow-flare slamming in head seas. Opposite of flare is tumblehome (side shell curves inward as it rises).
examiner_focus: Precision on the collision bulkhead's position (0.05L to 0.08L abaft the forward perpendicular, or 0.05L+3m) beats a vague "5-8% of length" -- these are two distinct regulatory limits, not one range.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Survey of a hollow rudder & possible effects/repairs
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Survey of a hollow rudder** (common to both sittings):
- Visual inspection for cracks/corrosion, and alignment — checked against the **rudder-stock/pintle axis and the jumping (lifting) clearance**, not against the ship's mast.
- Water-entry check in dry dock: open top and bottom plugs; water draining out indicates a breach.
- Pressure/leak test: rudder filled via the plug to a specified head (classically ~2.45–2.46 m, often referenced to the deepest waterline as required by class), watched for a pressure drop or water issuing from the lower plug. An air/vacuum test is a common alternative.
- Thickness gauging on older vessels/visible rust, to measure corrosion loss.
- Clearance measurements — pintle-to-bush (longitudinal/transverse), jumping clearance at the pintle, rudder-carrier bearing wear-down.
- Sacrificial anode condition, replaced if wasted.
- Stock keyway condition and coupling-bolt tightness.
- Percussion (hammer) testing for delamination/weakness.
- Freedom-of-movement / hard-over-to-hard-over check.

**(b-i) Effects if watertight integrity is compromised** (Dec 2017 framing): water floods the hollow rudder, greatly increasing its submerged weight and overloading the pintle/bearings and steering gear (higher torque demand, risk of overload or seizure); internal corrosion accelerates unseen; trapped water can produce a free-surface/list-trim effect if the volume is significant; and in freezing conditions, ice expansion within the rudder can split the plating.

**(b-ii) Repairs that may need to be carried out** (Jul 2021 framing):
- Corrosion treatment or plate section replacement.
- Gouging/grinding of cracked welds/plating, re-welding to a class-approved procedure with controlled pre-/post-heat, NDT after repair.
- Bearing/bush/sleeve replacement where wear or clearances exceed limits.
- Straightening of bent (unfractured) stocks — hot or cold, in an approved workshop.
- Twisted stocks: <10° may be reused (possibly new keyway); more severe requires annealing/replacement.
- Anode renewal, and a re-pressure-test before undocking, witnessed by the surveyor.
examiner_focus: Alignment is checked against the rudder-stock/pintle axis and jumping clearance, not the ship's mast -- a commonly wrong answer. Also note the (b)-part genuinely differs by sitting: sometimes "effects of lost integrity," sometimes "repairs required."

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Watertight/weathertight doors & bilge injection valve
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Watertight doors** are critical barriers preventing flooding spread between compartments, maintaining buoyancy/stability. A watertight door withstands a static head of water from either side without leakage, sized to the pressure at its location (per the subdivision/damage-stability calculation). Fitted below the bulkhead/freeboard deck — shaft tunnels, ballast tanks, engine room bulkheads, pipe tunnels.

**(ii) Weathertight doors** ensure water won't penetrate the ship in any sea condition (gaskets/cleats), but aren't designed for a sustained head — only brief submersion — and also give fire/smoke containment. Fitted on the freeboard/weather deck and superstructure — main decks, accommodation entrances, bridge entrances, engine room entrances.

**(b)** A bilge injection valve gives emergency bilge-pumping capacity: it lets the main sea water pump remove high volumes of floodwater directly from the engine room in a collision/grounding. It's a normally closed, screw-down non-return (SDNR) valve (often red-handled) on the suction of the largest-capacity sea water pump, diameter typically ≥2/3 of the main sea suction, handwheel high and accessible.

Testing: screen the strainer at the bilge injection suction; open the valve and confirm free operation/spindle condition; start the main sea water pump and close the main sea chest valve to draw suction from the bilge; monitor pressure gauges and confirm overboard discharge; close the bilge injection valve, re-open the sea chest, log the test, replace the valve seal. Never leave the valve cracked open in service — if the non-return element passes, the sea floods the bilge — confirm it shuts tight after testing.
examiner_focus: The bilge injection valve must be described as a screw-down non-return valve on the main SW pump suction, never left cracked open in service -- stating why (a passed non-return element would flood the bilge) is the mark-earning detail.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Five terms for hull distortion in heavy seas
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
1. **Hogging** — longitudinal bending, midship: a wave crest amidships lifts the centre, producing tensile stress at the deck and compressive at the bottom.
2. **Sagging** — longitudinal bending, midship: waves lift the ends while the midship sinks, producing compressive stress at the deck and tensile at the bottom.
3. **Racking** — transverse shear/deformation from rolling or uneven wave action, the rectangular midship section trying to distort into a parallelogram. Concentrates at the corners — beam knees, tank-side brackets, frame/beam connections — worst rolling in light/ballast condition.
4. **Panting** — localized dynamic stress: in-and-out flexing of shell plating near bow/stern from changing water pressure while pitching.
5. **Whipping** — transient, high-frequency longitudinal vibratory bending of the hull girder (2-node mode), triggered by slamming/bow-flare impact, decaying afterward; the hull vibrates at its natural frequency. (Springing describes steady, wave-excited vibration rather than transient.)

Pounding/slamming or pitching are also accepted as a sixth "condition of distortion" if a different term is wanted.
examiner_focus: Distinguishing whipping (transient, slam-triggered vibration) from springing (steady, wave-excited vibration) is what separates a strong answer from a bare list of five terms.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Distortion effects & the structure that resists them
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a) Racking** — dynamic transverse deformation from rolling. Resisted by transverse bulkheads, side frames, beam knees and pillars, tank-side brackets, web frames and deck transverses — the corners are where it bites hardest.

**b) Panting** — in-and-out shell flexing near bow/stern from pitching. Resisted by panting beams/stringers, breast hooks and panting frames in the fore/aft peaks, deep (panting) floors in the peaks, reduced frame spacing forward.

**c) Pounding** — repetitive bow slamming, localized stress. Acts over the flat of bottom in the forward ~25–30% L. Resisted by solid plate floors at every frame, intercostal side girders (≤~2.2 m apart), increased bottom-shell thickness, reduced frame spacing (~700 mm).

**d) Water pressure effect** — hydrostatic pressure increasing with depth, perpendicular to the hull below the waterline. Resisted by hull plating/stiffeners (longitudinal and transverse framing) and transverse bulkheads/internal framing.

**e) Drydocking stresses** — imposed by keel/bilge blocks in dry dock, peaking at the keel during the critical period as the stern lands first. Resisted by the keel structure (centre girder, floors), strong transverse framing, and the double bottom acting as a stiff grillage with the side girders.
examiner_focus: Drydocking stress peaking at the keel during sternframe touch-down is the point most candidates miss when the question extends beyond the usual racking/panting/pounding trio.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Ballast Water Management Convention
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** The BWM Convention 2004 aims to prevent the spread of invasive aquatic species and pathogens via ballast water, and to protect marine biodiversity and coastal environments from non-native species introduction.

**b) D-1 vs D-2:**
- **D-1 (exchange)** — open-sea exchange, ≥200 NM from land and ≥200 m depth (or, where impracticable, as far as practicable but never less than 50 NM/200 m depth), with volumetric exchange efficiency ≥95% (flow-through method, ≥3× tank volume pumped through). D-1 is being phased out.
- **D-2 (treatment)** — approved BWMS meeting discharge limits: <10 viable organisms/m³ (≥50 µm); <10 viable organisms/mL (10–50 µm); <1 CFU/100 mL toxicogenic *V. cholerae*; <250 CFU/100 mL *E. coli*; <100 CFU/100 mL intestinal enterococci. Full D-2 compliance required from **8 September 2024**.

**c) Documentation:**
1. **IBWM Certificate** — confirms compliance, issued by RO on behalf of flag state, states the standard (D-2) met.
2. **Ballast Water Management Plan** — vessel-specific procedures in a language the crew understands.
3. **Ballast Water Record Book** — logs all operations and deviations.
4. **Type Approval Certificate** for the BWMS.
5. **Ballast Water Reporting Form** — required by some ports on arrival.
6. Additional: Certificate of Calibration, training records, and (post-2020 amendments) a **Commissioning Test Report** (validation sampling) recorded before the BWMS is relied on for compliance; exemption documentation where applicable.
examiner_focus: The D-2 full-compliance date (8 September 2024) and the exact discharge limits by organism size class are what separate a full-marks answer from a vague "meets IMO standards."

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Anchor cable attachment & chain locker
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** The bitter end is secured via a bracket/retaining-pin arrangement (e.g. a weak-link bracket or slip — a senhouse slip or clenched ring with a release pin) that can be operated from **outside** the enclosed chain locker, usually from the deck/compartment above. Emergency release: remove a safety pin and drive out the locking pin with a dedicated red emergency sledgehammer. The release must not require entering the locker, since it's an enclosed space.

**b)** Chain lockers are emptied via a dedicated drainage eductor — a high-velocity fire-main jet creates suction drawing water/mud/silt from the sump, effluent mixing with motive water before overboard discharge, with fire main water flushing remaining sediment. Restrictions:
- Chain washed down thoroughly as hauled out, removing sediment/organisms.
- Rinsing/pumping prohibited in port (non-native species risk).
- At least monthly, rinsing/pumping as far from shore as possible and, where feasible, not in US federally protected waters/special areas.

**c)** Dangers entering a chain locker (COSWP): oxygen deficiency/asphyxiation — chiefly from rusting of chain/locker steel consuming oxygen; toxic/flammable gas accumulation; inadequate ventilation; slip/trip/fall/entrapment (especially shifting chain). Entry requires a full enclosed-space-entry permit (gas test, ventilation, standby man).
examiner_focus: The bitter-end release must be operable from outside the enclosed locker (never requiring entry) -- stating this explicitly, plus naming rusting of chain/locker steel as the oxygen-depletion cause, are the key marking points.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · In-water survey of a very large carrier
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
An In-Water Survey (IWS) inspects underwater hull parts while afloat, replacing one of the two required 5-year bottom inspections within the special-survey cycle, generally for ships under 15 years old (older vessels at class discretion). The ship must carry the IWS class notation, an approved high-resistance coating, and marked draught/ID points; the survey cannot proceed if significant damage is suspected or hull Conditions of Class are outstanding.

- **Preparation** — plans of external hull features below the sheer strake plus a key plan (frames/bulkheads/weld lines/openings); procedure pre-approved by the Classification Society; hull markings identified.
- **Cleaning** — diver-towed, hydraulically operated Brush Kart (three brushing heads) clears fouling.
- **Internal inspection** — complementary tank/space examination confirming no significant damage.
- **Documentation** — Master's declaration of no damage/grounding/unreported incidents; no outstanding hull CoC.
- **Vessel condition** — light draught, sheltered waters.
- **Survey vehicle** — self-propelled, steerable; long-range low-light TV camera (steering/distortion), close-view high-res colour camera (coating/weld seams), 35 mm still camera, ultrasonic thickness probe, depth/speed indicators, umbilical to the survey boat, buoyancy spheres/compressed air for recovery.
- **Survey boat** — control console (monitor, thickness printer, recording), diver communication, vehicle control.
- **Method** — certified divers, two-way CCTV, guide the vehicle along the shell expansion plan following weld runs/features; record video and thickness readings. Divers also measure stern tube bearing wear-down, rudder bearing/pintle clearances, and inspect sea chests, valves, propeller, shaft, stern seals, anodes, rudder and coupling bolts. Thickness gauging of suspect areas and rudder/stern-tube wear-down by divers is **mandatory**; the surveyor must witness in real time.
- **Outcome** — diving company submits a final report; surveyor reviews and, if requirements are met, endorses the Class Certificate for the Intermediate Bottom Inspection. Significant damage requires dry-docking instead.
examiner_focus: Stating that thickness gauging and rudder/stern-tube wear-down by divers is mandatory and witnessed in real time by the surveyor -- not just "video is recorded" -- is what earns full marks here.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Classification of ships & the notation +100A1
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Ships are built to classification society rules for:
- **Safety and integrity standards** — rules for design/construction/inspection ensure sound hulls, machinery and propulsion.
- **Regulatory compliance** — SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, Tonnage, COLREGS require adherence to a recognized class society.
- **Insurance and finance** — lower premiums; required by banks financing the vessel.
- **Quality control and certification** — surveyors monitor construction against approved drawings/rules.
- **Operational requirements** — the certificate proves seaworthiness, needed by charterers, bankers, ports.

**b) +100A1** (Lloyd's Register) — highest classification for a seagoing ship, steel, special survey, unrestricted worldwide service, approved equipment:
- **+ (Maltese Cross)** — built under special survey to the Society's Rules, to the Committee's satisfaction.
- **100** — historically LR's character figure for a ship built and eligible as first-class in the Register, suitable for sea-going service at the structural strength standard for unrestricted navigation.
- **A** — hull and appendages built to the society's rules and maintained in good, efficient condition.
- **1** — anchoring/mooring equipment (cables, hawsers) in good, efficient condition, complying with the Rules.

The notation is usually followed by a service/type notation (e.g. "Oil Tanker, ESP") and sometimes (E) for equipment to rule. Other societies use equivalent symbols (e.g. DNV's "✠1A").

**c)** A ship remains in class via initial, annual, intermediate, periodic, renewal and special surveys on a 5-year cycle, with maintenance/repairs/upgrades approved by class (PMS compliance) — plus no overdue surveys or outstanding Conditions of Class, prompt repair of damage affecting class, and ISM/audit-regime compliance. Otherwise class may be suspended or withdrawn.
examiner_focus: Breaking the notation into its four distinct elements (+/100/A/1), each with its own meaning, is required for full marks -- a single-sentence "it means the ship is classed" answer loses most of the available marks.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Class A bulkheads & ventilation (structural fire protection)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** A Class A bulkhead is a structural division of steel/equivalent non-combustible material, suitably stiffened, preventing passage of smoke and flame for a designated time in the standard fire test (SOLAS **II-2**). Requirements: steel/equivalent non-combustible, securely stiffened; capable of holding smoke/flame for the full 60-minute fire test regardless of insulation suffix; insulated so the average unexposed-side temperature doesn't rise more than 139°C, and no single point (incl. joints) more than 180°C, within: A-60 (60 min), A-30 (30 min), A-15 (15 min), A-0 (0 min). **The suffix number is the insulation period only — flame/smoke integrity is held for the full 60 minutes regardless of suffix.**

**b)** Ventilation design to prevent fire/smoke spread:
- Division by Main Vertical Zones — ducts serving one MVZ shouldn't pass through another; where they must, robust fire-resistant insulation prevents heat transfer across the boundary.
- Automatic fire dampers with manual operation from both sides and open/closed indicators, on ducts through fire divisions.
- Steel (or equivalent non-combustible) duct material.
- Atriums within Class A enclosures with smoke extraction (detector-activated, manual override, sized to exhaust the volume in ≤10 min).
- Ability to shut fans down immediately, cutting oxygen and preventing smoke circulation; a dedicated safety centre (SOLAS II-2 Reg 23) manages doors/dampers/detection.

**c)** Integrity at ventilation penetrations is maintained by insulated steel sleeves, ducts welded directly to the bulkhead, insulation matched to the bulkhead rating, or automatic fire dampers — preserving the boundary for the full 60 minutes. Ducts >0.02 m² require an insulated steel sleeve unless the duct itself is steel; ducts >0.075 m² require automatic fire dampers, manually operable from both sides with an open/closed indicator.
examiner_focus: The insulation suffix (A-60/A-30/A-15/A-0) is only the TIME the 140 degC/180 degC temperature limit is held -- flame and smoke integrity itself is always maintained for the full 60 minutes regardless of suffix, a distinction frequently missed.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Bulkheads, wing tanks & double-bottom purposes
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*(Note: the Jul 2025 sitting uses a slightly different mark split — 3/3/1/3 instead of 2/2/2/4 — for the same four question parts; content below already covers all four parts and needs no change.)*

**a)** Liquid carriers are divided by longitudinal bulkheads to improve structural strength, reduce free-surface effect, and allow multiple cargo grades — strengthening against bending/racking, preventing excessive listing, aiding cargo weight distribution and damage stability.

**b)** Ore carriers are fitted with wing tanks primarily because dense ore stows low, making the ship excessively stiff with a very short, violent roll period; ballasting the upper wing/topside tanks raises KG, lengthening the roll period and easing accelerations. Wing tanks also give self-trimming hopper geometry, ballast space, and double-skin protection against grounding/collision.

**c)** Double-bottom tanks in dry cargo ships, beyond liquid carriage, provide longitudinal strength, protect the hull in grounding, improve stability, give a foundation for cargo/machinery, and enable damage control by preventing flooding of the holds above.

**d)** Transverse watertight bulkheads:
1. Subdivision for flood control.
2. Structural strength/rigidity, resisting racking.
3. Fire subdivision.
4. Structural support for decks above.
The collision bulkhead and after-peak bulkhead are themselves SOLAS-required examples; total number is set by the floodable-length/subdivision calculation.
examiner_focus: For ore carriers, the real reason for wing tanks is raising KG to lengthen an otherwise dangerously short, stiff roll period -- "extra ballast space" alone misses the stability-physics point being tested.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Single vs twin propeller/rudder (wide-beam vessel)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** A single propeller/rudder is often unsuitable for a large, wide-beam cargo vessel because a wide, full hull produces a very non-uniform (high-block) wake at a single centreline screw — driving vibration, cavitation and reduced open-water efficiency, while the rudder behind it is partly shadowed. Achieving the required thrust would also need an exceptionally large screw diameter, risking cavitation and possibly exceeding available draught/immersion; a correspondingly massive single rudder would impose impractical bending moments on the stock and hydraulic loads on the steering gear.

**b)** Twin propeller/twin rudder offers superior manoeuvrability and low-speed handling (crabbing via differential thrust), redundancy (one set compensates if the other fails), better wake equalization (screws sit further outboard in cleaner flow) reducing fuel consumption/vibration, and shallower required draught per propeller. Trade-offs worth noting: higher build/maintenance cost, extra appendage drag, and a single screw is usually more efficient per kW in deep water. The "improved stability/roll" claim is weak — twin shafts give little roll damping — so lead with redundancy, manoeuvring and shallow-draught benefits rather than stability.
examiner_focus: Leading with "improved stability/roll" as a twin-screw advantage is weak -- twin shafts give little roll damping. Examiners want redundancy, wake-field uniformity, and shallow-draught benefit foregrounded instead.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Container-ship strength with large hold openings
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Removing the deck for cargo access leaves an open hull section with low torsional stiffness, vulnerable to twisting (warping) in oblique/quartering seas. Strength is built in as follows:

- **Torsion box (wing tanks)** — box girders running longitudinally along the top of the side shells, re-closing the section for torsional rigidity.
- **Transverse box sections at hatch ends** — join the torsion boxes together at each hatch, closing the loop and restoring torsional strength along the length — the central mechanism the question tests.
- **Double hull and double bottom** — rigid base/side structure for damage stability and longitudinal strength (keel, bottom shell, tank top, side shell, deck stringer plates, deck longitudinals).
- **Longitudinal framing** throughout, in high-tensile steel, for large bending moments.
- **Deep transverse bulkheads/webs** between holds for transverse strength.
- **Minimized bilge strake** — angled/rounded bottom-to-side transition to maximize stowage.

Construction uses the "box girder" method, verified by FEM. Hatch corners are a known fatigue hot-spot from stress concentration — radiused and insert-plated, checked by FEM.
examiner_focus: The core mechanism is torsional warping from the open deck section -- transverse box sections at the hatch ends closing the loop is the actual answer, not just naming "torsion box" without explaining why one is needed.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Noise levels on ships
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** The unit is the decibel, expressed as **dB(A)** — A-weighted to match human ear frequency response, filtering low/high frequencies people hear poorly.

**b)** Per the IMO Code on Noise Levels (MSC.337(91), mandatory under SOLAS II-1/3-12): hearing protection mandatory at/above **85 dB(A)** with warning signage; 80–85 dB(A) requires protectors available and information given; daily exposure limit LAeq(24) = 85 dB(A). **c)** Crew awareness: mandatory regulatory compliance, PPE training (earmuffs/plugs), warning signage, routine inspections — covering noise-induced hearing loss, fatigue and stress risks.

**d)(i) Diesel generators** — modern low-noise engine/fan design, optimized cooling-fan blades, high-performance exhaust silencers, vibration isolation (rubber/spring mounts). Strongest single measure: resilient/double-elastic mounting on a common raft with floating floor plus an acoustic enclosure/lagging.

**(ii) Ventilation fans/trunkings** — high-efficiency low-noise aerodynamic fan blades on anti-vibration mounts, flexible duct connectors preventing vibration transmission, acoustic duct linings, plus splitter/attenuator silencers with reduced air velocity.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Six degrees of motion & the structure that resists them
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Three translational — surge (fore-aft), sway (side-to-side), heave (vertical); three rotational — roll (longitudinal axis), pitch (transverse axis), yaw (vertical axis). Only heave, roll and pitch have a hydrostatic restoring force; surge, sway and yaw have none and are instead resisted/controlled by propulsion, the rudder/steering gear and mooring — not by structure.

**b)** Roll → bilge keels, fin stabilisers, anti-roll tanks. Pitch and heave (and the slamming/panting they cause) → strengthened bottom forward, bulbous bow, panting stringers/beams, deep floors. Yaw → rudder and steering gear (a control-device response, not structural resistance). Surge/sway have no dedicated resisting structure — managed by propulsion/mooring, though the double hull/bottom and continuous strength members (sheer/bilge/garboard/keel strakes) give general support through all motions.
examiner_focus: Only heave, roll and pitch have a hydrostatic restoring force -- surge, sway and yaw are managed by propulsion/rudder/mooring, not resisted by structure. Treating all six as "structurally resisted" is the main trap.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Hull stresses in heavy weather & the structure that resists them
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Longitudinal — hogging/sagging. Transverse — racking (worst at beam knees, tank-side brackets). Local — panting (fore-end shell flexing) and pounding (slamming impacts forward). Water pressure effect — hydrostatic pressure perpendicular to the hull below the waterline, increasing with depth.

The dominant heavy-weather case is longitudinal bending of the hull girder — stillwater bending moment + wave bending moment (hogging on a crest amidships, sagging in a trough) — together with shear (greatest near the quarter-length points) and, in oblique seas, torsion (important for open-deck ships). Deck/bottom section modulus is sized to this combined bending moment — why continuous longitudinal material is provided.

**b)**
1. Hogging/sagging → continuous longitudinal members: thickened sheer/bilge/garboard/keel strakes, deck stringers, HT steel, longitudinal bulkheads, deep double-bottom girders.
2. Racking → reinforced transverse bulkheads with large brackets, deep web frames, beam knees, deck/bilge brackets, rounded sheer strake, torsion-box double-bottom.
3. Panting/pounding → panting stringers/beams, reduced frame spacing (900→700 mm), deep plate floors, intercostal stringers on strengthened pillars/wash bulkhead, thickened bottom shell with intercostal girders (≤~2.2 m apart).
4. Water pressure → V-shaped hull sections, reduced forward flare, robust welding with combined longitudinal/transverse framing.
examiner_focus: The dominant heavy-weather case is combined longitudinal bending (hogging/sagging) plus shear near the quarter-length points -- many answers jump straight to panting/pounding and skip this primary loading case.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12/Q.13 · Watertight-door classification, hazardous closure & safe passage
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Classification.** Two schemes answer this, and stating both covers either reading of the question. SOLAS II-1 classifies watertight doors by *operating type*: **Class 1** (hinged), **Class 2** (power- or hand-operated), **Class 3** (power-operated, also closable remotely from the bridge). Separately, doors are categorised by *how they may be used at sea*: **Type A** — may be left open, closed only in an emergency; **Type B** — normally kept closed, may be opened for access to the adjacent compartment; **Type C** — kept closed at all times, opened only briefly for personnel to pass through; **Type D** — closed before the voyage commences and kept closed throughout navigation.

**(b) Circumstances requiring all watertight doors closed** when conditions are potentially hazardous: heavy weather, or where depth of water is less than three times the draught; proximity to underwater hazards, port limits, or compulsory pilotage waters; restricted visibility, high traffic density, or any other factor constituting a hazard.

**(c) Safety features of the operating system** (Dec 2020 framing): audio/visual warning — an alarm sounds and a light flashes for a few seconds before, and throughout, a remote closure; dual-position controls on both sides of the bulkhead so personnel can open and pass through from either side, with a local override to hold the door open; delayed/controlled closure — each power door takes 20–40 seconds to close under local/hand operation, while the bridge master switch must still be able to close *all* doors within about 60 seconds; a local control lever on either side that can open the door even while remote bridge closing is active; bridge position-indication for every door; and closure force/edges limited to avoid trapping personnel.

**(c-variant) Safe passage through a hydraulically operated watertight door** (Dec 2023 framing — explaining to a new crew member): confirm the bridge master mode switch is at "local control" before opening (else the door re-closes on releasing the local handle); locate controls, check local and remote indicators; open and wait until fully open; pass through quickly using the handles, watching footing; close after passing and wait for full closure/green light; **never pass through a moving door** (fatal crush risk); **never attempt to stop a closing door**. Emphasise doors stay closed at sea for watertight integrity, and confirm the crew member can operate it safely before leaving them to it.
examiner_focus: The 20-40 second single-door closure time and the ~60 second bridge-master-switch all-doors time are two different figures for two different situations -- conflating them is the most commonly flagged error.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Overhaul of ship-side valves in dry dock
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Information for the docking company: a comprehensive valve list (location/frame number, type, ID, means of closure, diameter, flange PCD) with a marked-up sea-chest plan; scope of work (cleaning/inspection/packing/full overhaul including seat grinding/testing); materials/spares split (ship vs workshop); isolation and safety procedure; critical timing for opening and refitting valves against the docking schedule.

**b)** Overhaul: dismantle (isolate, remove cover/gland packing/spindle, remove the valve chest if needed); clean/inspect (remove rust/corrosion, check seating face, lap the seat/disc until a continuous contact band is achieved — engineer's-blue check); reassemble (coat exposed steel, renew studs/nuts/joints to correct grade/torque, anti-seize on threads); function-test (smooth operation, hydrostatic test at test pressure).

Precautions before returning to service: since ship-side valves below the deepest waterline are classed items, the Classification Society surveyor should witness the open-up, seat condition, reassembly and hydrostatic test before the dock is flooded — the single most important precaution. Also: confirm positive isolation/lock-off while open; refit and prove blanks/spectacle isolation are removed; record test pressures in the dry-dock/class report; secure the valve in its required position with locking washer/nut tight and handle greased; final tally confirming every sea connection is closed and locked before flooding.
examiner_focus: The single most important precaution is class surveyor witnessing of the open-up, seat condition and hydrostatic test before the dock floods -- omitting the surveyor's role is the main source of lost marks.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Tank inspections, erosion in ballast tanks & enclosed-space entry
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Structural integrity (cracks/fractures/grooving); general corrosion, pitting, blistering, coating condition; condition of cargo equipment; sacrificial anode condition; internal pipework/fittings condition; tank opening/manhole integrity.

**b)** Erosion is found beneath the bell-mouth — strictly **erosion-corrosion**, where high-velocity suction flow/vortex action mechanically sweeps away the protective coating/scale and bare steel then corrodes; at the bottom plating and suction wells, where sediment retention promotes microbiologically induced corrosion; and — the point most often missed — along the **waterline/part-full band**, where the tank is alternately wet and dry, typically the worst corrosion zone in a ballast tank.

**c)** Enclosed space entry (COSWP): risk assessment (oxygen depletion, toxic/flammable gas, slip/trip/entrapment) and entry plan; ventilate, isolate connecting pipelines/machinery, lock-out/tag-out; test atmosphere at top/middle/bottom with calibrated detectors, keep ventilation running, re-test periodically and after breaks — proceed only once O₂ reads 20.9% and hydrocarbon/toxic gases (H₂S, CO) are within limits; permit time-limited, re-validated after breaks. Rescue equipment ready (tripod, stretcher, SCBA, first aid) with a designated rescue party; entrants wear PPE (personal gas monitor, harness, lifeline, torch, EEBD). Complete an Enclosed Space Entry Permit with a toolbox meeting. Trained attendant posted at the entrance maintaining communication; evacuate immediately if anyone feels unwell or an alarm sounds. Secure the space and close the permit on completion.
examiner_focus: Erosion beneath the bell-mouth is technically erosion-corrosion -- mechanical stripping of the protective layer by high-velocity flow, not simple wear -- and precision on this mechanism is what examiners look for.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Repair of defects on a solid propeller in dry dock
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a) Bent blades** — hot or cold straightening with a hydraulic press/alignment tools, propeller secured, worked back to shape without over-stressing (manganese/nickel-aluminium bronze propellers are straightened with local pre-heat rather than truly cold, to avoid cracking). Inspect for fatigue/damage, then balance.

**b) Damaged blade tips** — metal-arc welding, building up material (cast steel/copper alloys as appropriate), shaped/finished to match. Must comply with **IACS UR W24** (the propeller-repair rule — UR W27 relates to stern-tube/shafting, so W24 is the correct citation); welding below the 0.7 radius needs class approval. Post-repair dye-penetrant NDT (the propeller is non-magnetic, so MPI isn't used).

**c) Missing blade pieces** — assess salvageability first. Blades divide into three stress zones: Zone A (highest — root/lower radii, ~0.4–0.6R on the driving face) — welding prohibited or needs special approval; Zone B (intermediate — approved procedure); Zone C (outer/tip — most freely repairable). If salvageable, build up by metal-arc welding with compatible material, or cast a new piece to fit.

Common to (b)/(c): approved welding procedure and a welder qualified for the specific alloy, controlled pre-heat/interpass temperature, stress-relief after major build-up, dye-penetrant NDT, then balance the whole propeller (static normally, dynamic for high-speed/CPP) before class sign-off.
examiner_focus: The propeller blade's three stress zones (A/B/C by radius) determine whether welding is prohibited, needs special approval, or is freely permitted -- omitting the zone-based restriction is the main gap in weaker answers.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Double-bottom fuel tanks — sounding pipes, air pipes & vent design
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Weighted cocks are self-closing when not in use, keeping water out (preventing fuel contamination), while the weight allows smooth operation when sounding. The sounding pipe runs from the tank top to a striking plate on the tank bottom (absorbing the rod's impact), stays as straight as practicable, and terminates at an accessible deck level with the self-closing weighted cock.

**b)** Air pipes equalize pressure (preventing build-up/vacuum during pumping) and ventilate the tank (letting gases escape, reducing explosive-atmosphere risk). Cross-sectional area must be ≥1.25× the filling-line area, so the air pipe is never the restriction during bunkering.

**c)** i. **Heavy weather** — gooseneck shape, the upward bend preventing water entry in heavy seas. ii. **Fire** — flame arresters/screens preventing external flame reaching flammable vapour inside. iii. **Bunkering** — vents at the tank's highest point, terminating on open deck with suitably sized save-all trays at the base; per ICLL, coamings at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck, before a float-type automatic self-closing device plus flame screen.
examiner_focus: The air pipe cross-sectional-area rule (at least 1.25x the filling-line area) is a specific figure worth quoting exactly, ensuring the vent is never the bottleneck during bunkering.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Watertight doors — factors, operating requirements & hazards
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**a)** Number/size factors: subdivision/damage-stability requirement (a door only where genuinely needed for access through a bulkhead); operational function/access (restricted to essential points — shaft tunnel, duct keel, passenger passage — opening kept minimal); structural strength of the bulkhead (limited so proper framing/reinforcement is maintained).

**b)** Below the weather deck: kept closed at sea, used only for passage and closed immediately after; two power sources including independent emergency power giving at least three complete open-close cycles against a 15° list with no main power (~1 hour independent operation). Capable of closing simultaneously from the bridge master switch within **60 seconds** with the ship listed to 15° — this is the *all-doors-together* time. An individual power-operated sliding door, operated alone, must close in **20–40 seconds** with the ship upright — examiners specifically check that these two closure times aren't conflated. Doors also operable locally from both sides, with a bridge master mode switch offering "local control" vs "doors closed." Audible alarm 10 seconds before and during closure; remote visual open/closed indicators at bridge and control station.

**c)** Hazards and mitigations:
1. **Crushing injury/fatality** — never pass through a moving door; never stop a closing door.
2. **Hand/body pinch points** — mandatory two-handed, hold-to-open local handle operation.
3. **Sudden automatic re-closure** — confirm the bridge master switch is at "local control" before opening; check indicators.
4. **Lack of situational awareness** in noisy spaces — adherence to procedure/signage, no carrying loads alone while passing, regular training/familiarization.
examiner_focus: The 20-40 second single-door time versus the ~60 second bridge master-switch all-doors time recurs here too -- state both explicitly rather than one figure covering both situations.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Watertight & weathertight doors — function/location; scuppers & freeing ports
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Watertight doors.** Critical safety barriers fitted below the waterline/freeboard deck,
in any opening that would otherwise compromise the ship's watertight subdivision — shaft
tunnels, ballast tank access, engine room bulkheads, pipe tunnels. Function: contain flooding to
the damaged compartment, limiting its spread and preserving buoyancy and stability. Defined as
withstanding a design head of water from either side without leakage.

**(a)(ii) Weathertight doors.** Fitted above the waterline, in exposed positions subject to
adverse weather — main decks, accommodation entrances, navigation bridge entrances, engine room
entrances — designed so water will not penetrate the ship in any sea condition, including brief
submersion. They do **not** provide fire or smoke containment; that is the separate function of an
A- or B-class fire division, and should not be attributed to a weathertight door.

**(b) Why scuppers and freeing ports must be operational at all times.** Water drainage — scuppers
drain water accumulating on deck before it adds weight, promotes waterlogging, or causes
corrosion/structural damage. Stability — if freeing ports fail, water pools on an enclosed deck,
increasing free-surface effect, raising the centre of gravity, and reducing effective freeboard by
the added weight. Safety during operations — a clear, drained deck reduces slip/fall risk for crew
in rough weather. Regulatory compliance — scuppers and discharges are governed by **ILLC
Regulation 22**, and freeing ports separately by **ILLC Regulation 24** (these are two distinct
regulations, not both Reg 24); non-compliance risks penalty and detention.
examiner_focus: Weathertight doors do NOT provide fire/smoke containment -- that is a commonly stated but incorrect claim; that function belongs specifically to A- or B-class fire divisions.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Double-hulled oil tankers — mid-ship section, evolution, disadvantages
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** [Sketch — mid-ship cross-section: main deck/deck stringer plate/sheer strake; port and
starboard cargo tanks either side of the longitudinal bulkhead; topside and hopper wing water
ballast tanks; inner shell and inner-bottom shell; double bottom with centre and side girders,
floor plating; bilge strake, garboard strake, keel strake, duct keel — as per original figure.]

**(b)** Double-hulled tankers evolved to minimise the risk of a massive oil spill following
grounding, collision, or internal tank rupture. **MARPOL Annex I, Regulation 19** mandates
double-hull (or equivalent) construction for oil tankers, with single-hull tankers phased out
under **Regulation 20**; the US **OPA 90** imposed an equivalent domestic requirement — both driven
by the 1989 **Exxon Valdez** grounding. The extra, protective inner layer prevents cargo-tank
rupture during lower-energy impacts.

**(c) Four disadvantages** (the strongest, examiner-credited points, ahead of the weaker
cost/stability framing): explosion/atmosphere risk in the double-hull void spaces, which must be
inerted, ventilated and gas-monitored — the *Bow Mariner* incident is the cautionary reference;
difficult access for survey, and a high incidence of corrosion in the narrow, poorly-accessible
ballast voids; greater steel weight, reducing deadweight/cargo capacity for a given displacement;
and the cost of coating and maintaining the additional ballast spaces, on top of the general
increase in construction and operational cost.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Bulk carrier — inspection of the upper topside areas (as Chief Engineer)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
As Chief Engineer, inspection of the upper topside areas focuses on mitigating corrosion, ensuring
watertight integrity and confirming structural reliability: hatch covers and coamings — cracks,
deformation and wastage, particularly at hatch corners, a high-stress area; watertight integrity —
condition of rubber gaskets, packing and sealing arrangements on all hatch covers; securing
devices — cleats, hinges and quick-acting cleats operational and well-greased; air pipes and
sounding pipes to the topside tanks — corrosion, particularly at the threads, and verification that
the **automatic (float) closing devices** function correctly to prevent water ingress; deck
structures — wasting or pitting of deck plating around crane foundations, pedestal mounts and
windlasses; ventilation and access — manholes, ladders and tank access safe, clean and
unobstructed; underside of the upper deck — buckling or corrosion of deck stiffeners; load line
marks — clearly visible, unaltered, not obscured by corrosion or paint, and still compliant;
firefighting system — hoses, nozzles and sprinklers ready and compliant; lighting — emergency and
work lighting functioning.

What converts this from a generic deck inspection into a genuinely bulk-carrier-specific answer is
naming the structure unique to bulkers: the **topside (sloping) tank internal structure and
brackets**; the **cross-deck strips and hatch-end beams**; and especially the **transverse
corrugated bulkheads and lower stools between holds** — the classic No.1/No.2 hold
progressive-flooding failure mode on bulk carriers. On a single-side-skin bulker, add the
**side-shell frames and their end brackets**, a known wastage hotspot.
examiner_focus: Naming the transverse corrugated bulkhead between Nos. 1 and 2 holds -- the classic progressive-flooding failure point on bulkers -- is what converts a generic deck inspection into a genuinely bulk-carrier-specific answer.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Scuppers vs freeing ports; tanker handrails
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** Scuppers sit close to the superstructure to drain water away from weathertight doors and
vertical structures instantly — superstructures create corners and obstructions where water
gathers, so scuppers protect entrances and deckhouses from waterlogging there. Freeing ports are
sited along open bulwarks at open areas of the weather deck: large openings sized to rapidly
release large volumes of shipped seawater before it can pool and compromise stability. Both are
critical to maintaining stability and preventing structural damage.

**(b)** Essential at all times for: water drainage (scuppers clear deck water before it adds
weight or causes waterlogging/corrosion); stability (failed freeing ports let water pool,
increasing free-surface effect, raising COG, and reducing freeboard by the added weight); crew
safety in rough seas (a clear deck reduces slip/accident risk); and regulatory compliance —
scuppers/discharges fall under **ILLC Regulation 22**, freeing ports under **ILLC Regulation 24**
(two separate regulations).

**(c)** Beyond personnel safety, tankers fit **open handrails rather than solid bulwarks** on the
main cargo deck because open rails let any green sea clear the low-freeboard deck edge
immediately rather than trapping it. This avoids the extra stress a retained mass of water would
add to the hull, and prevents the raised COG, free-surface effect and reduced freeboard that
retained water would otherwise cause; it also saves steel compared with a solid bulwark. (Note:
the usual credit of freeing-port area as a fraction of bulwark length does not apply where open
rails are fitted instead of a bulwark.)
examiner_focus: Scuppers fall under ILLC Regulation 22 and freeing ports under Regulation 24 -- two separate regulations. Citing both under one regulation number is a recurring error across several questions in this topic area.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Container-ship cargo hatch covers — testing, load transfer, wear
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Water-tightness testing.** The primary method is a **hose test**: a nozzle of ≥12 mm bore,
held ≤1.5 m from the hold/cover joint, delivering a water jet at **≥2 bar**, traversed slowly along
the full joint — any leak into the hold indicates a gap. Supplementary methods: a **chalk test**
(checks compression of the sealing rubber against the landing bar, but proves compression, not
tightness, on its own), an **ultrasonic tightness test** (the preferred method at sea — gives a
quantitative leak reading, is independent of weather, and can be run with cargo already loaded),
and visual inspection from inside the closed hold for light penetration.

**(b) Load transfer.** The weight of the lift-away pontoon-type cover and stacked containers is
carried through **weight-bearing pads** fitted between the hatch cover and the coaming, which
relieve the elastomeric neoprene seal of load. These pads are local, separate supports — not a
continuous rigid connection — so the cover can move slightly relative to the coaming as the hull
deflects in a seaway, without transmitting damaging stress into the surrounding structure.

**(c)** [Sketch — hatch-cover support: weight-bearing pads at the cover/coaming interface, cleat,
neoprene rubber seal.] Type and location of wear damage: **hatch support (bearing) pads**, at the
cover/coaming interface — repeated container-stack loading and vibration wears steel or specialty
(elastomeric/copper-alloy) pads, reducing pad height, causing improper cover seating, uneven load
distribution and stress cracking in adjacent steelwork; **hatch cover stoppers (restraining
devices)**, the longitudinal/transverse stoppers at the sides and ends — buffeting wear enlarges
clearances, letting the cover shift and deforming the stoppers and surrounding plate; **sealing
arrangement (periphery)**, the rubber gasket and compression/landing bar on the coaming — uneven
compression from pad wear causes permanent set, hardening or tearing of the seal, while the
compression bar itself thins from corrosion and friction.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Aluminium alloy in shipbuilding & welding aluminium panels
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Advantages:** light weight, corrosion resistance (aluminium forms a self-protecting oxide
film — it is not in fact rapidly corroded in seawater), high versatility, recyclability.
**Disadvantages:** softer than steel; expensive; requires specialised welding technique; low
melting point and loss of strength in fire, requiring A-class insulation protection where used
in fire-rated divisions; higher thermal expansion than steel; and, the genuine corrosion risk,
**galvanic corrosion at aluminium-to-steel joints** — which must be isolated with insulation or an
explosion-bonded (bi-metallic) transition strip rather than joined directly.

**(b)** [Sketch — TIG welding: tungsten electrode, filler wire, shielding gas, arc, molten/solidified
weld metal.] Gas tungsten arc (TIG) welding uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with separate
filler wire, shielded by an inert gas — argon or helium — fed through an annular nozzle around the
electrode. It suits shop fabrication better than field work, since the gas blanket must be
maintained. DC (usually electrode-negative) or AC current may be used depending on material and
desired weld quality; for aluminium specifically, **AC TIG (or MIG) is used** so the cathodic
half-cycle of the AC waveform breaks up aluminium's tenacious oxide film. The work must be cleaned
of oxide beforehand, and pre-heat/interpass temperature controlled to avoid porosity and
lack-of-fusion. Argon suits general use; helium gives a hotter arc for thicker sections.
examiner_focus: "Corrodes rapidly in seawater" is a common but misleading claim -- aluminium is actually corrosion-resistant via its own oxide film. The real risk is galvanic corrosion at aluminium-to-steel joints, which needs isolation.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Fatigue cracks in a ship's hull & drydock hull inspection
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** Fatigue cracks arise from repeated cyclic loading — wave, wind and manoeuvring forces
producing fluctuating stress that accumulates damage over the vessel's operational life; poor
design or inadequate reinforcement at critical areas creates stress concentrations that promote
crack initiation. The locations where cracks are actually found, and the ones that score marks,
are: hatch-corner and deck-opening-corner radii; bracket toes and the ends/heels of longitudinals;
intersections of longitudinals with transverse webs; lightening-hole edges; side-shell-frame end
brackets on bulk carriers; and weld toes with undercut or poor profile. The underlying driver is
**stress concentration combined with cyclic stress range**, not primarily material weakness.

**(b)** A comprehensive drydock hull inspection: thorough visual examination of the entire hull
surface for corrosion, pitting, deformation, visible cracks or weld defects; inspection of
protective coating condition (peeling, blistering, or wear exposing bare metal); **ultrasonic
thickness gauging** at representative locations to identify wastage below acceptable limits;
close-up inspection of welded joints, brackets and supports — using a borescope where access is
difficult — with **MPI or dye-penetrant** for surface-crack detection and **UT** for thickness and
embedded defects; assessment for deformation from grounding or collision, including hogging or
sagging along the ship's length; opening sea chests for cleaning/inspection and checking sea
valves for wear or corrosion; and systematic recording of all findings, referenced to the class
**Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP)** close-up survey and thickness-measurement reporting
requirements.
examiner_focus: Naming specific high-incidence locations (bracket toes, longitudinal/web intersections, lightening-hole edges) scores far better than the generic "areas of stress concentration."

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Aft-end vibration at full-service speed — report to the Engineer Superintendent
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*(Original answer format retained: a report to the Superintendent Engineer.)*

**Possible causes:** propeller issues (imbalance, damage, cavitation); shaft misalignment between
the propulsion shaft and stern tube bearings; structural resonance in the aft section (stern
frame, hull, supporting structures prone to resonance/harmonic amplification); machinery imbalance
in rotating equipment; insufficient vibration damping. The technically decisive cause to name is
**blade-rate (blade-passing frequency) resonance**: the propeller's exciting frequency = shaft rpm
× number of blades, and when this coincides with a natural frequency of the aft hull/sterngear the
resonance and harmonic amplification described above results — cavitation-induced pressure pulses
on the hull plating above the propeller are the usual driving mechanism.

**Recommendations for this vessel:** propeller inspection and balance/cavitation check; alignment
check between propulsion shaft and stern tube bearings; structural analysis of the aft section to
identify and address resonance; machinery alignment and balancing; enhanced vibration damping; sea
trial and performance monitoring after remedial work.

**Recommendations for sister vessels under construction:** increase propeller tip clearance from
the hull; fit a highly-skewed propeller to soften pressure pulses; adjust the number of blades to
shift blade-rate frequency away from the hull's natural frequencies; run a finite-element vibration
analysis at the design stage; standardise machinery alignment/balancing procedures; fit real-time
vibration monitoring; document lessons learned for future construction projects. These specific
measures are what earn the marks, rather than a generic "reinforce the structure."
examiner_focus: Naming blade-rate (blade-passing frequency) resonance explicitly -- shaft rpm times number of blades -- is the technically decisive point; a vague "propeller imbalance" answer misses the resonance mechanism being tested.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Transverse watertight bulkheads — reasons, definition, minimum number/location, testing
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*(These are the same core topic asked in two slightly different part-breakdowns across the source
sittings; merged into a single canonical answer covering every part asked in either version.)*

**Reasons for fitting transverse watertight bulkheads:** flood prevention/containment — dividing
the ship into separate compartments limits the spread of water if the hull is breached, preserving
buoyancy and survivability; structural integrity — bulkheads act as strength members, effectively
as pillars supporting deck and tank tops and helping resist the hull's overall bending and shear;
stability improvement — additional support and reduced free-surface effect; fire containment —
bulkheads can serve as fire barriers restricting spread between compartments.

**What constitutes a watertight bulkhead:** a vertical partition designed to prevent water passing
from one compartment to another, built with minimal openings, of reinforced steel (or equivalent)
plating able to withstand the hydrostatic head of a flooded adjacent compartment without leakage
or structural failure.

**Minimum number and location:** for a ship with machinery amidships, typically **four** watertight
bulkheads minimum — collision bulkhead, after peak bulkhead, and one bulkhead at each end of the
machinery space; a ship with machinery aft needs a minimum of **three**. The number required
increases with ship length under class rules. The **collision bulkhead** is positioned not less
than **0.05L** and not more than **0.08L** (in some cases 0.05L + 3 m) abaft the forward
perpendicular, extending from the bottom of the hull to the upper (bulkhead) deck. The **after
peak bulkhead** encloses the stern tube and extends to at least the first deck above the load
waterline.

**Testing:** a **hose test** (water sprayed onto joints/seams) proves joint and seam tightness
only. The proper strength/boundary test of the bulkhead structure itself is a **fill (head) test**
— filling the compartment, or a test tank, to reproduce the design hydrostatic head — or an
**air/leak test** using a leak-indicating solution. State explicitly that the test reproduces the
design head; a hose test alone does not validate structural strength.
examiner_focus: A hose test only proves joint tightness, not structural strength -- the actual strength/boundary test is a fill (head) test to the design hydrostatic pressure, a distinction frequently missed.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Dry-dock specification — repair of ballast-tank shell damage, and costing factors

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Standing orders — serious fire in machinery spaces while in dry dock
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Standing orders should cover: **immediate response** — raise the alarm, notify bridge and dry dock
management with location and extent; **evacuation** — clear machinery spaces and adjacent areas,
muster at the designated assembly point and report to the supervisor; **firefighting equipment**
— use portable extinguishers (CO2 or foam) only if trained and it is safe to do so, without taking
undue risk; **isolation of equipment** — shut down machinery/electrical systems if safe, close
fuel oil, lube oil and other flammable-liquid valves; **communication** — maintain contact
throughout, reporting conditions and any trapped personnel to emergency services; **fire control**
— activate fixed firefighting systems if available, and assist firefighters with vessel layout and
hazard information; **post-incident actions** — account for all personnel, do not re-enter until
declared safe; plus training/drills, reporting procedures and safety-equipment checks as ongoing
measures.

The point that specifically carries marks for this question: **in dry dock, the ship's own fixed
CO2/sea-water fire main is normally out of action** — sea suctions exposed, systems isolated for
hot work — so primary fire cover comes from the **shore/yard fire main and the dock fire party**,
and the standing orders must state who supplies fire-fighting water in that condition. A hot-work
permit, continuous fire watch and boundary-cooling regime should be in force; the alarm must alert
both ship and yard; and escape routes and the muster point differ in dock — via staging/gangways
and typically a single brow. These dry-dock-specific points, not the generic fire drill, are where
the marks lie.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Defects in ballast-tank steelwork — causes, areas affected, minimisation
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Causal factors:** corrosion — general corrosion, pitting, and microbially-influenced
corrosion (MIC), worsened by inadequate coating and contaminants; poor maintenance — inadequate
tank cleaning/inspection, poorly secured manhole covers allowing water ingress; stress
concentrations at welds, fittings, or points where temporary lifting devices were used during
construction, compounded by repeated loading/unloading fatigue cycles; and operational practice —
improper or too-rapid ballasting/deballasting causing pressure surges and excessive force.

**(b) Areas most likely to be affected, and how indicated:** tank bottom plating — erosion/
corrosion from sediment accumulation and stagnant water, shown by visible rust/pitting and
confirmed by ultrasonic thickness measurement; weld seams — stress-concentration points, shown by
visible cracks/deformation and confirmed by dye-penetrant or ultrasonic NDT; tank-top/under-deck
plating and especially the **air–water interface ("waterline band")**, where alternating wet/dry
exposure with oxygen produces the worst pitting; horizontal surfaces — flange faces, brackets,
stiffener tops — that hold standing water; and around heating coils and the suction bell-mouth,
where erosion-corrosion is common.

**(c) Methods to minimise damage:** a rigorous inspection and maintenance schedule with routine
cleaning to remove sediment and contaminants; high-quality protective coatings as the primary
barrier — referencing the **IMO PSPC (Performance Standard for Protective Coatings)**, a 15-year
target-life coating system mandated for dedicated seawater ballast tanks; and **cathodic
protection** (sacrificial anodes or impressed current) as a complementary measure, not an
alternative — anodes only protect bare/holiday areas where the steel is wet, so coating and anodes
work together.
examiner_focus: The waterline/part-full band -- where alternating wet/dry exposure with oxygen gives the worst pitting -- is the area most often missed in favour of the more obvious tank bottom.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Hazards in enclosed spaces (oily bilge tank, ballast tank, refrigerated space) & entry procedure
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Hazards.** All three named spaces are, first and foremost, **oxygen-deficiency/enclosed-space
risks**, each with a specific additional hazard layered on top: **oily bilge tank** — oxygen
depletion from rusting/oxidation of the steel, plus flammable hydrocarbon vapour as a fire hazard
in contact with hot surfaces or sparks, the oil itself acting as an added fuel source; **ballast
tank** — stagnant water and organic material generating toxic gases such as hydrogen sulphide or
methane, posing a serious health risk; **refrigerated space** — often limited ventilation risking
low oxygen levels, worsened by any refrigerant leak, which is asphyxiant, or toxic if ammonia.

**(b) Procedures prior to entering enclosed spaces (per COSWP 2025):** pre-entry planning — a risk
assessment identifying hazards, and an entry plan; ventilation and isolation — ventilate
thoroughly, isolate connecting pipelines/machinery with lock-out/tag-out; atmosphere testing — test
with calibrated gas detectors at top, middle and bottom of the space, **in the fixed order O₂ →
flammable → toxic**, entering only when **O₂ = 20.9% by volume**, flammable gas **< 1% LFL**,
**H₂S < 5 ppm** and **CO < 30 ppm**, keeping ventilation running and re-testing periodically;
safety equipment — rescue equipment ready at the entrance with a designated rescue party, and PPE
including a personal gas monitor, harness, lifeline, safety torch and EEBD; and an enclosed-space
entry permit with a toolbox meeting, plus a trained attendant posted at the entrance maintaining
radio communication and continuous monitoring.
examiner_focus: All three spaces are fundamentally oxygen-deficiency risks first -- treating the oily bilge tank as purely a fire hazard, without naming oxygen depletion from rusting, is the most common omission.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Twin skeg rudders — reasons for fitting & advantages of the installation
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
A **skeg** is a structural extension of the hull that carries or encloses the propeller shaft and
supports the rudder. A **twin-skeg** arrangement places two shafts and propellers beneath a wide,
shallow, full-form hull — used on large bulkers, car carriers and LNG ships, where a single screw
would be too large or too heavily loaded for the available draught.

**(a) Reasons for fitting:** improved manoeuvrability at low speed — two rudders give more
effective directional control for docking and narrow channels; redundancy — loss of one
rudder/propeller line still leaves propulsion and steering available via the other; and — the
dominant genuine reason — a shallower draught than a single-screw arrangement of equivalent power
would require.

**(b) Advantages for modern large-cargo-capacity vessels:** a better, more uniform wake field
giving higher propulsive efficiency with less cavitation and vibration; the ability to fit two
smaller-diameter propellers under limited draught; true propulsion redundancy; more even
distribution of structural load across the bottom; reduced vulnerability to losing all propulsion
or steering to a single incident; and flexibility for naval architects to optimise the hull form
for cargo capacity while still achieving good propulsive efficiency. ("Increased stability against
rolling" is a weak claim for twin skegs — they add little roll damping, and should not be led
with.)
examiner_focus: "Increased stability against rolling" is a weak claim for twin skegs -- they add little roll damping. Lead instead with the genuine advantages: wake-field uniformity, shallower draught, and propulsion redundancy.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Propulsion efficiency — ducted propeller (Kort nozzle) and vane/Grim wheel
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Ducted propeller (Kort nozzle).** [Sketch — cylindrical duct surrounding the propeller.] A
Kort nozzle surrounds the propeller with a cylindrical duct that streamlines inflow, accelerates
water through the propeller disc, and reduces tip-vortex losses. It is most beneficial on
**heavily-loaded propellers at low speed/high thrust** — tugs, trawlers, DP vessels — where it
raises bollard pull; on a fast, lightly-loaded merchant ship, the duct's own drag at speed can
cancel the gain. Advantages: increased thrust, reduced power consumption, improved low-speed
manoeuvrability. Disadvantages: added weight and complexity, cost, potential for cavitation if
poorly designed.

**(b) Vane or Grim wheel aft of the propeller.** [Sketch — vane wheel mounted aft of the
propeller.] The Grim vane wheel is **free-running, not fixed**: its smaller inner radius acts as a
turbine driven by the propeller's rotational slipstream, while its larger outer radius acts as a
propeller, adding thrust — recovering rotational (swirl) energy that would otherwise be lost as
wake turbulence. Advantages: energy recovery, reduced wake turbulence, enhanced thrust at low
speed. Disadvantages: increased drag, maintenance requirements, space constraints, and a known
weakness of **blade fatigue/fracture in service**.
examiner_focus: The Kort nozzle only helps heavily-loaded propellers at low speed/high thrust -- on a fast, lightly-loaded merchant ship its own drag at speed can cancel the gain, a nuance often left out of a purely descriptive answer.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Preventing hull fractures due to corrosion fatigue in modern shipbuilding practice
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**Corrosion fatigue** is fatigue cracking accelerated by a corrosive environment, so the measures
adopted must address stress and corrosion together, not separately: **material selection** —
high-tensile steel, corrosion-resistant alloys, and corrosion-resistant coatings; **design** —
eliminating stress concentrations at source through generous radii at hatch corners, soft/scarfed
bracket toes, and avoiding notches; **assembly sequence** — prefabricated, pre-cut plates aligned
and welded using established procedures, approved consumables and controlled parameters, via
standard shipbuilding processes such as **submerged-arc, flux-cored, or manual metal arc welding**
(laser welding is not standard practice for ship hulls); **weld quality** — good weld profile and
full penetration, avoiding undercut, and grinding or peening weld toes at fatigue-critical details;
**post-weld treatment** — stress relieving, heat treatment, or shot blasting to remove surface
irregularities; and **surface protection on completion of construction** — thorough surface
preparation (abrasive blasting or high-pressure water jetting to remove contaminants, rust and mill
scale), followed by a **multi-layer coating system** (primer, intermediate coat, topcoat, typically
epoxy-based) referenced to the **IMO PSPC** standard for ballast tanks, plus **cathodic protection**
(sacrificial anodes or impressed current). Ongoing regular inspection, maintenance and periodic
recoating complete the picture — keeping the surface coated is what prevents corrosion pits from
initiating the cracks in the first place.
examiner_focus: The question specifically asks about corrosion FATIGUE -- a strong answer addresses stress-concentration design and corrosion protection together as one mechanism, not as two separate lists.

look for, is that it sets a **5-year certificate cycle** with annual/intermediate/renewal surveys
timed so that the different conventions' surveys fall together within a survey window of roughly
**±3 months** about the certificate's anniversary date. This delivers efficiency (fewer redundant
surveys), consistency (uniform assessment regardless of flag state), simplification (clearer
administrative requirements), and interoperability (mutual recognition of surveys and certificates
between classification societies and regulators).

**(b) Load-line certificate — items inspected and how kept in compliance.** The load-line renewal
survey occurs every 5 years, with annual surveys in between. Items inspected: hull condition
(corrosion, damage, structural integrity affecting buoyancy and stability); load-line marks
(correctly displayed, visible, accurately reflecting the assigned freeboard); hatch covers and
other closing appliances (watertight, in good working order); freeing ports and scuppers
(unobstructed, functioning); up-to-date stability information; and maintenance records confirming
regular inspection. These items are, precisely, the **conditions of assignment** of freeboard, and
compliance is maintained through the regular survey cycle, ongoing maintenance protocols for all
load-line fittings, documentation updates, and crew training/awareness.
examiner_focus: HSSC's defining mechanism is aligning survey timing across conventions within a roughly plus-or-minus 3 month window of the certificate anniversary -- naming this window, not just "it harmonises surveys," is the examiner-credited point.
