canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · TBT antifouling ban; alternative coatings; underwater coating selection
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** The IMO has banned tributyltin (TBT) antifouling coatings under the **AFS Convention**
(International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001; in force
2008), because TBT is highly toxic to non-target marine organisms, causes hormone disruption —
**imposex** (masculinisation) in molluscs such as the dog whelk, and shell malformation in
oysters — and bioaccumulates up the food chain.

**(b) Alternative coatings:** **copper-based coatings** (base element copper, releasing copper
ions toxic to fouling organisms — a biocide, but less harmful than TBT); **biocide-free
foul-release coatings** (based on silicone or fluoropolymer — non-toxic, low-surface-energy
polymers that prevent firm attachment without leaching any chemical).

**(c) Considerations in selecting an underwater coating:** environmental impact and regulatory
compliance (minimal harmful leaching, AFS Convention compliance); fouling resistance and
durability over the intended drydocking interval; self-polishing versus hard/ablative behaviour;
application process (surface preparation, curing time); compatibility with the existing coating
system; cost-effectiveness; and the ship's speed and activity profile — a slow-moving or
frequently-idle vessel fouls faster and needs a coating matched to that duty cycle.
examiner_focus: Naming the specific mechanism (imposex -- hormone-driven masculinisation in molluscs such as the dog whelk) rather than a vague "harmful to marine life" is what separates a strong part (a) answer.

canonical_answers.title: Q.13 · Propeller slip — definition, calculation, conditions affecting it
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** Propeller slip is the difference between the theoretical distance a propeller should
advance in one revolution, based on its pitch, and the distance it actually advances through the
water, expressed as a percentage of the theoretical distance. Two distinct figures should be
distinguished: **apparent slip** = (engine speed − ship's speed) / engine speed, where engine
speed = pitch × rpm and ship's speed is read from the log; **real slip** = (engine speed − speed of
advance Va) / engine speed, where Va = V(1 − w) and w is the wake fraction. Real slip is always
positive; apparent slip can go negative in a following current or sea — the **wake fraction** is
what makes apparent and real slip differ.

**(b) Conditions affecting slip, with reasons:** hull condition — fouling or damage increases drag
and hence slip; vessel speed — for a displacement ship, slip typically falls as speed rises;
propeller design — diameter, pitch and blade shape affect efficiency, with a larger-diameter
propeller generally showing less slip; environmental conditions — wind, current and sea state, a
head sea or adverse current increasing resistance and hence slip; and draught/displacement, since
a deeper, heavier ship experiences more slip. (Reasoning based on displacement-versus-planing
mode belongs to fast planing craft, not a normal displacement merchant ship, and should not be
applied here.)
examiner_focus: Distinguishing apparent slip from real slip (via the wake fraction) is the key technical point -- many candidates only know one definition and conflate the two.

canonical_answers.title: Q.14 · Large fixed-bladed propellers — effect of hull fouling, clean/ballast operation, light propeller
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Effect of hull fouling.** Marine growth — barnacles, algae — accumulating on the hull and
propeller increases drag and reduces propeller efficiency, so more power is needed to achieve the
same thrust, resulting in decreased speed and increased fuel consumption at a given rpm.

**(a)(ii) Operation in clean hull, ballast condition.** With minimal drag and the ship in a
balanced ballast condition, the propeller achieves optimal thrust with lower power requirements,
enhancing both speed and fuel efficiency. [Sketch — engine power (% kW) vs %rpm, showing
clean/ballast, fouled, and light-running curves about MCR.] The diagram is read in terms of engine
margin: a propeller is **"light"** when it absorbs less torque for a given rpm, so its
power-demand curve sits to the right (higher rpm) of the design curve, letting the engine reach MCR
rpm and full power before the torque/overload limit is reached. The reserve between the running
point and that limit is the **Light Running Margin (LRM)**, typically **~4–7%**.

**(b) Why fitting a light propeller may be beneficial.** As the hull and propeller foul, and in
adverse weather, the demand curve shifts left into **"heavy running"** — the LRM is precisely what
lets the engine still develop full power in that condition without exceeding the torque limit or
overloading. Naming "heavy running" explicitly and quoting the LRM figure — rather than generic
statements about manoeuvrability and fuel economy — is what scores the marks. A light propeller
also helps vessels navigate critical speed ranges more safely, since the increased power margin
reduces the risk of damaging vibration, adapting to hull fouling and adverse weather to ensure full
power remains available when needed.
examiner_focus: Naming "heavy running" explicitly and quoting the Light Running Margin figure (roughly 4-7%) is what scores the marks in part (b), rather than generic statements about fuel economy or manoeuvrability.

canonical_answers.title: Q.12 · Hazards in enclosed spaces (oily bilge tank / ballast tank / chain locker) & entry guidance
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Hazards, with reasons:** **oily bilge tanks** — oxygen depletion from rusting/oxidation of the tank steel, compounded by flammable hydrocarbon vapour given off by residual oil and sludge, a fire/explosion risk in contact with hot surfaces or sparks, with the oil itself acting as an added fuel source; **ballast tanks** — oxygen deficiency from rusting of the large internal steel surface area, plus stagnant water and trapped organic material generating toxic gases such as hydrogen sulphide or methane; **chain lockers** — oxygen deficiency, chiefly from rusting of the chain and locker steel consuming oxygen, plus risk of toxic/flammable gas accumulation given poor natural ventilation in the enclosed, awkwardly-shaped space, and physical hazards from shifting chain, slip/trip and entrapment risk in a confined space with limited access.

**(b) Guidance to be followed before entry into an enclosed space (per COSWP):** a pre-entry risk assessment and entry plan; thorough ventilation and isolation of connecting pipelines/machinery with lock-out/tag-out; atmosphere testing with calibrated gas detectors at top, middle and bottom, in the fixed order **O₂ → flammable → toxic**, entering only when **O₂ = 20.9% by volume**, flammable gas **< 1% LFL**, **H₂S < 5 ppm** and **CO < 30 ppm**, keeping ventilation running and re-testing periodically and after any break; rescue equipment ready at the entrance with a designated rescue party, and PPE including a personal gas monitor, harness, lifeline, safety torch and EEBD; a full **enclosed-space entry permit** with a toolbox meeting; and a trained attendant posted at the entrance maintaining continuous radio communication and monitoring throughout.
examiner_focus: Chain lockers are an oxygen-deficiency risk chiefly from rusting of the chain itself -- easy to miss if a candidate defaults only to "toxic gas" reasoning for this space.

canonical_answers.title: Roll reduction systems (bilge keels, passive anti-roll tanks, fin stabilisers)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**Roll reduction systems — bilge keels, passive anti-roll tanks, fin stabilisers**

*Covers two mark-split variants seen across sittings: a 5/5 split (bilge keels + passive tanks only —
Jul 2016, Mar 2018, Dec 2025) and a 4/6 split ("bilge keels stating advantages" + "TWO other methods
of roll reduction" — Dec 2019, Mar 2022). The content below serves both: use (a)+(b) for the 5/5
form, or (a)+(b)+(c) selecting any two of the "other methods" for the 4/6 form.*

**(a) Bilge keels.** Narrow fins or plates attached longitudinally along the turn of the bilge, on
both sides of the hull, running roughly amidships. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance
— generating eddies and vortex shedding — as the vessel rolls, which damps the roll amplitude by
dissipating energy rather than by any restoring moment. Advantages: low maintenance compared with
active systems; no internal components, so no loss of cargo or operational space; relatively
inexpensive to fit and maintain; and — the point examiners specifically look for in a
comparison — bilge keels work at **zero speed**, unlike fin stabilisers.

**(b) Passive (uncontrolled) anti-roll tanks.** Free-flooding tanks, typically port and starboard
or a U-tube arrangement, in which water shifts from side to side as the vessel rolls. The tank is
tuned so that the water's natural sloshing period is close to the ship's natural roll period; the
phase lag between the water's motion and the hull's motion creates a moment that opposes the roll
and damps its amplitude. Advantages: mechanically simple, no power or control system required, and
relatively cheap to install. Disadvantages: the tank's free surface always **reduces GM** — it does
not increase stability, and any answer listing "increased stability" as an advantage of a passive
tank is self-contradictory, since the same free-surface effect is also correctly listed as a
disadvantage. The real benefit is roll-amplitude damping near the tuned frequency, accepted at a
small, known GM cost. A second trap worth stating explicitly: because the tank is tuned to a
*specific* natural roll period, if that period shifts with a change in loading condition (a change
in GM), the tank can become mismatched — losing its damping effect, or in the worst case,
reinforcing rather than opposing the roll. Delayed response time and the significant space taken up
by the tank are the other recognised disadvantages.

**(c) Active fin stabilisers** (the usual choice for the second "other method," 4/6-split variant).
Underwater, wing-like appendages fitted to both sides of the hull below the waterline. Sensors
detect the ship's roll and command hydraulic cylinders to tilt the fins, generating hydrodynamic
lift that opposes the roll — analogous to how an aircraft wing generates lift, but here the "angle
of attack" is actively commanded rather than fixed. Advantages: superior roll reduction compared
with passive systems, improving both safety and comfort, and highly efficient at cruising speed.
Disadvantages: increased drag and fuel consumption from the extended fins; risk of damage
(vulnerable to grounding, fishing gear, ice); and — the standard advantage/disadvantage comparison
examiners expect — **fins are ineffective at low speed and at anchor**, since they rely on forward
way through the water to generate lift, whereas bilge keels and passive tanks continue to work at
zero speed.
examiner_focus: The passive anti-roll tank does NOT increase stability -- its free surface always costs some GM; the genuine benefit is roll-amplitude damping near the natural roll period. Listing "increased stability" as an advantage is a direct contradiction examiners catch.

canonical_answers.title: Passenger ship fire/smoke spread prevention (Class A/B bulkheads, A-60 test, penetrations)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**Passenger ship structural fire protection — Class A/B bulkheads, spread prevention, A-60 test, penetrations**

*Covers three mark-split variants: the generic 10-mark "describe the requirement for preventing the
spread of fire and smoke" (Jul 2018, Mar 2021, Mar 2022, Oct 2024); the 7/3-split "spread prevention
+ A-60 fire test" (Mar 2019); and the 3/3/2/2-split "Class A/B bulkhead definitions + penetrations"
(Oct 2020). All parts needed for any variant are covered below.*

**Class A bulkheads (definition, 3 marks where asked separately).** Structural divisions
constructed of steel or an equivalent material, suitably stiffened, designed to prevent the passage
of smoke and flame for the full standard fire test. Insulated with non-combustible material such
that the average temperature on the unexposed side does not rise more than 140°C above the original
temperature, and no single point (including joints) rises more than 180°C, within the time denoted
by the class's insulation suffix: **A-60** (60 min), **A-30** (30 min), **A-15** (15 min), **A-0**
(0 min). The suffix is the *insulation* time only — flame and smoke integrity itself is maintained
for the **full 60 minutes regardless of suffix**, a distinction worth stating explicitly since it's
frequently conflated.

**Class B bulkheads (definition, 3 marks where asked separately).** Approved non-combustible
materials (combustible veneers may be permitted under conditions), offering integrity against the
passage of flame for at least **30 minutes**. The average unexposed-side temperature must not rise
more than 140°C above the original, and no single point may exceed **225°C**, within the class's
suffix time: **B-15** or **B-0**.

**Penetrations — retaining integrity (2+2 marks where asked separately).** Where a Class A bulkhead
must be penetrated: **doors** must be of the same class rating as the division they penetrate (an
A-60 bulkhead needs an A-60-rated door), self-closing, with hold-back permitted only via a fusible
link or remote-activated release — never a simple wedge or catch. **Ventilation trunking** is
fitted with an insulated steel sleeve at the crossing; where the duct breaches an A-class boundary,
an automatic, fail-closed fire damper is fitted, with position indication (open/closed) at the
control point.

**Preventing the spread of fire and smoke generally (the 7- or 10-mark framing).** The ship is
divided into fire zones by continuous Class A (or B, as applicable) bulkheads and decks, with every
joint, seam and penetration sealed to the same rating as the division itself — a single unsealed
gap defeats the whole division. This passive structure is backed by active measures: fire detection
(smoke and heat sensing giving early warning) and fire suppression (automatic sprinklers, foam
systems, or gas flooding in machinery and cargo spaces) to contain any outbreak within one zone
before it can spread to the next.

**Standard fire test for Class A-60 material (3–5 marks where asked separately).** The test
specimen must be representative of the actual construction, including any joints, built from the
approved materials; exposed surface area at least 4.65 m², with a minimum height of 2.44 m for
bulkheads or length of 3.04 m for decks. Bulkheads are tested vertically, decks/ceilings
horizontally. Thermocouples are placed at multiple points on the unexposed face, including at joints
and stiffeners, to monitor temperature throughout. The specimen is exposed in a furnace following
the standard **cellulosic (ISO 834) time–temperature curve** — reaching approximately **576°C at 5
minutes, 841°C at 30 minutes, and 945°C at 60 minutes**. (Note: "927°C" sometimes seen quoted as
"the" test temperature is actually roughly the *30-minute* point on this curve, not a fixed test
temperature — state the curve, not a single figure.) For A-60, the test runs the full 60 minutes;
throughout, unexposed-side temperature is logged against the 140°C-average/180°C-point limit, and
the specimen is watched for any opening — flaming on the unexposed face, or ignition of a
cotton-wool pad held against a gap, constitutes a failure of integrity regardless of the
temperature reading.
examiner_focus: The standard fire test follows the cellulosic (ISO 834) curve reaching about 945 degC at 60 minutes -- quoting "927 degC" as the test temperature (rather than roughly the 30-minute point on the curve) is a specific, gradeable error.
